title: Going to Europe and planning a record
summary: He has been abroad only with Lunceford; he would tour Europe for exposure and wants to record with a seven-piece group, cutting to five for travel.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well, now, let's see, we're getting near the end of this one. So that almost brings us up-to-date, doesn't it?
I don't know.
Oh, wait a minute. You did go to Europe, didn't you?
Yeah, I went with Lunceford in 19 --
Haven't you been with Black and Blue?
No, I only went over there with Lunceford.
That's the only time you've been?
That's the only time. Then I went out of the states again with Eddie to Canada for a week.
Yeah. Well, I was thinking that those guys in France that take these little groups and they would be interested in you.
(Inaudible) they want me to come over and I always said if I was going to go, I was going to contact you. But I'm always trying to prepare myself for something that other guys don't do, you know?
Well, that's a good thought.
In fact, (inaudible) three men, I might have something organized. I'd like to get a record out. Any

kind of little record (inaudible). That's their gimmick there. They do a little tour and they make a record. I don't know the financial details, but that guy who runs the tours on he's got loads of money.

Yeah, well,they -- plenty of them has tried to get me to come over, but I would go without management standing. I'm not that type of musician. See, I was a band leader. I'm not just a sideman and I learned a lot.
Well, actually, the way they --
Somebody else could do it, if they can, you know (inaudible).

Well, you could, with them, actually, you're fairly safe. I mean, there's all kinds of people been over for them and they've never had any trouble. I mean, it's not a big deal. I mean, that's the point. I don't know whether financially it would satisfy you, but I think you should --
Oh, well, when I go, I don't want to go for so much money. I want to go for the exposure and have something to offer, so they'll want you back.
Well, that's the way to look at it.
(Inaudible) record, organize. When you go in the studio, play it. Go in there and get a balance.
: There's six albums there from Norman Grantz recorded on tour this summer, all jam sessions, you know? And it's --
They make a little money on them, some kind of way, but I don't want to (inaudible). How do you think Ray Charles (inaudible) got a hit? (Inaudible). I'm telling you, he had a band.
: Well, I mean, jamming is all right, but, I mean --
Sure.
: -- you make six there with the same people -- Oscar Peterson --
Well, they never sound the same way? (Laughter.)
: Well --
I ain't seen too many jam sessions go over. I saw one go over and that was Lionel Hampton with Flying Home, you know, Lloyd _______.
: No, you could, you know, really it would be a good time to make a few organized records with six or seven pieces. That's what you want.
(Inaudible). See, I want to record with about seven pieces. But I can cut that so I can travel with five --
: Yeah.

-- and get the same effect (inaudible) that I would get on the record with the other guys, because you cut that expense and you have that sound, because they made records with Frank Sinatra and Ella and them. I heard them with a lot of fiddles. Them guys were out --
(End of Side 5).
